div.p: T h e object-oriented design methods and their CASE tools are widely used in practice by m a n y real-time software developers. However, object-oriented CASE tools require a n additional step of identifying tasks from a given design model. Task identification is usually performed in a n ad-hoc manner using hints provided b y h u m a n designers. In this paper, we present our ongoing research into schedulability-aware, automatic synthesis of multi-threaded implementation of a real-time object-oriented design. W e present several feasible i mplementation strategies and architectures. W e propose our approach to automatic implementation and address schedulability issues involved in our approach.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The object-oriented design methods and their CASE tools are widely used in practice in developing complex real-time systems. However, there is an important shortcoming in current object-oriented CASE tools for real-time systems. In object-orient design methodologies, it is not very clear and obvious how to translate an object-oriented design model into an imple-mentation when an underlying run-time system does not support active objects as a first-class entity. This is often the case in practical real-time operating systems since object-based kernels tend to be very slow due to indirect pointers and object references. Thus, object-oriented CASE tools require an additional step of identifying tasks.

In this paper, we present our ongoing research into schedulability-aware, automatic synthesis of multithreaded implementation of a real-time object-oriented design. We propose our approach to automatic implementation, present several feasible implementation architectures to support the proposed approach, and address schedulability issues involved in the approach.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 overviews the UML-RT design model and its CASE tool. UML-RT is our choice for a real-time object-oriented design model. Section 3 presents several feasible implementation strategies and our multi-threaded implementation architecture. Section 4 overviews our synthesis approach. Section 5 presents real-time schedulability issues involved in our approach. We conclude this paper in Section 6.

3 Multi-Threaded Implementation Architectures

div.head: Overview of UML-RT
div.p: UML-RT [8] is a specialization of UML [2]' and targeted for a category of systems that are characterized as complex, event-driven' and potentially distributed. The new concepts added to UML are derived from the ROOM [7] which is also an object-oriented modeling technique optimized for complex, event-driven realtime system.

The fundamental modeling element of UML-RT is a capsule. A capsule represents independent flows of control in a system and communicates with other objects only by sending and receiving messages through interface objects called ports. A capsule may possess internal structures so that it is possible to describe complex systems in a hierarchical manner.

Capsules and connections between capsules' ports construct a structure model. The behavior of each capsule is described by a finite state machine. A capsule's state is changed by a message arrival at a capsule's port. A message can be thought of as an event in that a message has only one method to trigger actions. Thus, we use the terms event and message interchangeably.

div.head: RoseRT and Run-Time Systems
div.p: RoseRT allows users to design an object-oriented real-time system by providing a visual modeling environment. It also allows them to automatically generate an executable program which is composed of application code, skeleton code, and run-time system service libraries. The core component of the RoseRT run-time system (RTS) is a controller object that dispatches messages to capsule instances. It takes the next message from a message queue and delivers it to the destination capsule instance by invoking the capsule's behavior described by a finite state machine. When there are multiple messages in the queue, it processes them according to their priorities. Thus, message priorities determine the priority of the action triggered by messages.

Depending on implementation strategies, there can be several implementation architectures for an executable program resulted from automatic code generation. The operation of the behavior model in realtime object-oriented modeling is based on event processing. As such, in a multi-threaded implementation architecture, each thread receives its associated messages and processes them one by one. By adopting different strategies for mapping messages (events) to threads, we can come up with as many implementation architectures. As addressed by Saksena et al. in [4],
there can be three different mapping strategies. They are summarized below. 0 Map all events associated with an object to a single thread.
0 Map all events in a transaction to a single thread.
0 Map all events at the same priority to a single thread.

We in turn call them (1) capsule-based, (2) transactionbased, and (3) priority-based mapping. Note that the priority-based mapping strategy can be applied with one of the other two mapping strategies. Our approach to automatic implementation is based on both the transaction-based and priority-based mapping strategies. by associating capsule instances with dynamically created, optional tasks and then inserting code incarnating capsule instances in initial state transitions of fixed capsule instances. This hurts one of the advantages of object-oriented design methodsseparation of design models and implementations. Nevertheless, this approach is effective to reduce blocking time due to priority inversion.

div.head: Transaction-Based Mapping
div.p: Each transaction in a system is a sequence of actions flowing through an end-to-end computation initiated by an external event. An action inside a transaction is triggered by an internal message. An external event rnay initiate a transaction or multiple transactions. We can derive a transaction in an automatic manner by building a tree tracing message flows.

A transaction may be associated with timing constraints such as periods and deadlines as in [3]. Interthread comniunicatiori can be eliminated and the design models become similar to those used in classical real-time scheduling theory. However, as will be discussed in later sections, it also incurs various complications when we attempt to obtain an automated and optimized implementation in a schedulability-aware manner.

Figure 1 shows the data structure of a message. Note that the message has a reference to a target active object (capsule instance). Figure 2 shows the basic code structure of each thread. Each thread waits for any external event (message) to be delivered. When an external event is delivered, the thread starts a new transaction. The inner while loop of Figure 2 (a) processes an event by invoking actions of a transaction. The run-to-completion semantics of UML-RT requires that the execution of each action be serialized by the mutes guarding an active object possessing the action (Figure 2 (b)). Figure 2 (c) shows the pseudo code of a function (Behavior 0) which implements the behavior represented by a finite state machineof an active object. This function selects an appropriate action from its active object by matching the port and signal of a delivered message with those of actions, and in turn compares the current state of its active object with the source state of the selected action. If no matched action is found, the delivered message is discarded. Note that the code generator synthesizes the code for each active object.

div.head: Proposed Approach
div.p: We are currently developing an approach that can automatically generate multi-threaded implementations from any given real-time object-oriented design. Our implementation strategy is the combination of transaction-based mapping and priority-based mapping.

Our approach is based on several assumptions. (1) All external events are periodic. (2) Message priorities are determined not at design time but at implementation time. Our goal is to automate the scheduling of messages through our approach without relying on fine-tuning of a design model. (3) Transactions that start from the same active object are mutually exclusive. This assumption does not impose serious limitations on the utility of our approach since most systems in practice meet this assumption.

Our approach is a three-step process: identifying (1) transactions, ( 2 ) logical threads, and then (3) physical threads. The first step derives transactions from a given design model as we explained in Section 3.2. The second step groups mutually exclusive transactions, merges them into a task, and assigns each task a priority. We refer to this task as a logical thread to differentiate it from a physical thread that actually comprises a final implementation. As a result, a task may have multiple scheduling attributes including periods, execution times, and the blocking times. Note that transactions in a task may have different periods and deadlines. Therefore, we need a new schedulability analysis algorithm that can take into account this new task model. We also adopt preemption threshold scheduling presented in [9]. We assign each logical thread the maximum preemption threshold. For this preemption threshold assignment, we also need a schedulability analysis algorithm considering the preemption threshold.

The final step merges logical threads into nonpreemptive groups [5, 61 according to their priorities and preemption thresholds. This step can significantly reduce the number of tasks. Each non-preemptive group becomes a physical thread. The end result of our approach is an automated implementation method which maps real-time object-oriented models to multithreaded implementations.

div.head: Blocking Time
div.p: In [3], Saksena et al. identified several sources of priority inversion that contributed to blocking time in applications designed under the ROOM model using the ObjecTime tool. These blocking sources are (1) two-level scheduling, (2) message passing, and ( 3 ) runto-completion. Blocking due to two-level schedulirig can be easily avoided with dynamic priority inanagement of the run-time system. Blocking due to iriterthread message passing is not present in transactionbased implementation architecture. However, the actions of a transaction may be blocked, due to the runto-completion semantics, by a lower priority action that shares the same active object. As explained in Section 3.2, transaction-based implementation architecture should use a mutex lock for each active object to keep the run-to-completion semantics. To reasonably bound this run-to-completion blocking time, we adopt the P C P E ( P C P Emulation) protocol. [l]. In PCPE, when a task is executing inside critical sections, its priority is unconditionally increased to the highest of the priority ceilings of all the mutexes owned by the task. We assign each mutex a priority ceiling equal t o the maximum preemption threshold of messages sent to the active object which possesses the mutex. With the PCPE protocol, blocking can occur only once when a transaction tries to start its execution. The worstcase blocking time is equal to the blocking time due to the preemption threshold scheduling.

div.head: Response-Time Analysis
div.p: As we mentioned in Section 4, to assign each logical thread a feasible priority and the maximum preemption threshold, we need schedulability analysis algorithms. Our schedulability analysis algorithms are based on a response-time analysis. Because a logical thread is a collection of transactions, it may have multiple scheduling attributes including periods, execution times, and the blocking times. The accurate and intuitive approach is to compute the response times of all transactions in each logical thread. However this approach may require too much computation time due to search space explosion, even for a system with a modest size. We are currently developing heuristic responsetime analysis algorithms for our task model.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have described our ongoing research into schedulability-aware, automatic synthesis of multithreaded implementations from real-time objectoriented design models.

There are several feasible multi-threaded implementation architectures depending on implementation strategies: (1) capsulebased mapping, (2) transaction-based mapping, and (3) priority-based mapping. Our approach for automatic implementation is based on both the transactionbased and the priority-based mapping strategy. Our approach is composed of three steps: identifying (1) transactions, (2) logical threads, and then (3) physical threads. Our approach introduce a new task model where each task is a collection of mutually exclusive tasks possessing different scheduling attributes such as periods, execution times, and blocking times. With this new task model, we are developing heuristic schedulability analysis algorithms.
